So the nagging moved. Every deadline now goes to your phone through notifications, where you control it one category at a time. Out of season the chat still gets a single save-the-date when something lands on the calendar. In season it gets nothing — you have real football to argue about.

Except on the day itself. If there are owners we could not reach on their phone, the chat gets one post naming exactly those owners and @-mentioning them. Not the whole league — the people who were about to miss it. Same for the Sunday lineup check: everyone with a broken lineup gets a private heads-up, and only the ones we couldn't reach get read out in front of everybody. The tagging stops the moment you subscribe, and when everyone has, the posts stop happening on their own.

The trade talk is staying right where it is. Schefter's rumor mill, the trade-block listings and the daily speculation are not deadlines — they are the reason people start deals, and they belong in the room where deals get made. Still capped at three a day, still four hours apart, still with a Trade Builder link on every one. Two league-wide announcements survive in season too: the trade deadline a week out, and a Throwback Week kickoff every Tuesday that reports how many teams have locked an era in and how many still need to pick.
Net effect: the bot says a lot less and the league says a lot more. Go pick your alerts.

title: Wait — So Do I Still Use MyFantasyLeague?
imageAlt: The new FAQ page, headlined “Wait — so do I still use MyFantasyLeague?”, with a short-version summary card underneath.
summary: Short answer: yes. MFL still runs the league and isn't going anywhere. The new FAQ lays out exactly which site does what, why both exist, and — the part worth reading — how an idea you post here turns into something that actually gets built.
description: It's a fair question and nobody had written the answer down. There's a URL you've used for twenty years and a newer one that keeps showing up in the group chat, and if you've been quietly wondering which of them is the real league, you weren't the only one. The FAQ settles it in one line: both, and neither is going away.

MyFantasyLeague is still the source of truth. It scores every game, stores the official rosters, and enforces the settings. That isn't a limitation we're routing around — a league this old needs a system of record that has already survived twenty seasons, and MFL has done that job the entire time without drama. The old site works. The MFL apps work. Your bookmarks work.

What's new is that the league also has its own app now. MFL has to serve every league on earth, so its screens are configurable rather than specific. Ours only has to serve this one, so it can be specific — which is how you get live scoring built for a phone on the couch, standings with the playoff math already done, and two decades of owner history that MFL has the data for but no page to show. The FAQ carries a plain table of who handles what, so you never have to guess where to go.

And then the part that is genuinely different: the person who can build your idea is in your league. Everyone has fired a feature request into a suggestion form and watched it vanish — not out of rudeness, just arithmetic. Post it on The Board instead and it gets read, argued about by the rest of the league, and — if it's good — filed as real work, usually inside a week. Then it turns up right here in What's New with your name on the thread that started it.
Rule changes still need their 75% vote per the constitution; The Board is where they get pitched, not ratified. Anything about the site itself needs no vote at all — just somebody willing to type it.

title: The AFL Gets a Suggestion Box
imageAlt: The Board on the AFL site — an empty idea feed reading “No ideas yet. Be the first to suggest something!” beside a sidebar explaining how it works.
summary: The Board — post an idea, the league argues about it, the Commissioner rules on it — is now open in the AFL, with its own ideas, its own comments, and its own everything. It starts empty, so somebody gets to be first.
description: The Board is the official place to pitch a rule change, report something broken on the site, or float an idea and see whether anyone else likes it. Post it, other owners comment and react, and the Commissioner sets a status on it — Under Review, Approved, Rejected, Implemented. Nothing disappears into a folder.

It's a board of the AFL's own. Every idea, comment, reaction and unread badge posted here lives in the AFL's own storage — nothing is shared with any other league, and nothing you post shows up anywhere else. It starts empty, which means somebody gets to be first.

The one thing that carries over from the constitution: a rule change still needs its 75% vote, 18 of 24. The Board is where the argument happens before the vote, not a replacement for it. Site suggestions have no such bar — the good ones just get built.
New to how any of this fits together? The FAQ explains what still lives on MyFantasyLeague, what lives here, and what happens to an idea after you post it.

title: Who's on the App, and Who's Still Living in a Tab
linkLabel: See the split on Owner Activity
summary: Owner Activity now knows whether a visit came from the site installed on a home screen or from an ordinary browser tab — with the platform behind it, an app-versus-browser share for the league, and a note on each owner's row saying which one they showed up on last.
description: An installed app and a browser tab are the same website wearing different clothes: same pages, same login, same everything the server can see. Which is why Owner Activity could tell you exactly when somebody last checked their roster and had nothing at all to say about how they did it — whether they tapped an icon on a home screen or dug the site out of a tab they had open since August.

Now it says. A new App vs Browser section up top splits every visit four ways — the installed-app share, the browser share, and how each of those breaks down for people signed in versus people just passing through — then goes platform by platform underneath: iPhone and iPad, Android, desktop, with a bar showing which way each one leans. And down in the Last Seen table, every owner's row now ends with where they turned up last: On App (iPhone / iPad) — 81% app.

The bookkeeping is deliberately thin. Signed-out visitors are counted, because an owner reading the league page without logging in is exactly the traffic the old counter never saw — but they are counted and nothing else: no page, no timestamp, no name. Two numbers go up, and the only other thing that touches the database is a one-minute counter that stops anyone hammering the endpoint, filed under a scrambled version of their address rather than the address itself.
imageAlt: The App vs Browser section of Owner Activity: four cards reading Installed App 52%, Browser 48%, Signed In 1,612, Signed Out 278, above a table splitting visits by platform — iPhone / iPad, Desktop and Android — each with a bar showing how far it leans toward the app.

title: The Guy You Want Already Belongs to Somebody
summary: Tap a rostered player anywhere on the site and the modal now offers a handshake: Trade for him. It drops you into the Trade Builder with his owner on one side, him already in the deal, and you on the other — no team picker, no scrolling a roster to find the name you were just looking at.
description: When we put a Claim button inside the player card, it fixed exactly one problem: the free agents. Tap a name nobody owns and you can bid on him then and there. Tap a name somebody does own — which is to say most of the league — and the card just sat there with his stats on it, admiring the problem. You knew who had him. You knew what you wanted. And the site's answer was to make you go find the Trade Builder yourself, pick his team out of a dropdown, then hunt his name down a roster you had already been staring at.

Now there's a second button. Rostered players get Trade for him, with the owner named right on it — "Build a trade with Vitside Mafia" — so you find out who you're negotiating with before you commit to the click. It opens the builder with his club loaded, him already sitting in the deal, and your team seated across the table. The first decision you make is what you're willing to give up, which is the only decision that was ever interesting.

The card knows which of three people you are. He's yours: nothing to offer, and no button pretending otherwise. He's unowned: the Claim or Bid button you already know. He's somebody else's: the handshake. You never see the wrong one, because the site works it out from the actual rosters rather than guessing from whichever page you happened to open him on — the same page can hand you all three in a row and get all three right.

AFL owners, the conference line holds, because your league's trades do. A player rostered over in the other conference isn't a trade you're allowed to make, so the button doesn't appear and doesn't tease you — what you get is the copy of him inside your own conference, if there is one, and the claim button if there isn't. Go browse somebody else's roster or run down the player list and start tapping names.
imageAlt: The player card for Matthew Stafford, headed "Rostered by Vitside Mafia". Below it two side-by-side action cards: "Watch player" with an eye icon, and a highlighted "Trade for him" with a handshake icon reading "Build a trade with Vitside Mafia".

title: Twenty-Four Teams. One Ballot. Your Call.
summary: The Owners' Poll comes to the AFL. Every Tuesday The Pecking Order ranks all 24 by the numbers; now you rank your top 10 — your own team included, if you think you belong there — and the room's answer runs in Thursday's column right beside the machine's.
description: For a year now, The Pecking Order has told you every Tuesday who the best team in this league is, and every Tuesday somebody in the chat has explained why it's wrong. Fine. Put it on the record. The Owners' Poll opens with the column each Tuesday and closes Thursday at the week's first kickoff, and what comes out of it publishes in that same issue, next to the algorithm, so the week's real story becomes the room versus the machine.

Rank your top 10. Not seven — this is a 24-team league, and ten is what it takes to actually say something about a field this size. Your own team is on the ballot like everybody else's; nobody is stopping you from putting Smokane first, and the Homer Index is going to notice if you do. Tap the teams in the order you rate them, shuffle them until it's right, and change your mind as often as you like until the ballot shuts.

One ballot, both conferences. The AL doesn't get its own poll and neither does the NL. The column already ranks all 24 in one list, and half the fun of this league is arguing whether an American League team that beats up on the American League would survive a month in the National. Now there's a table where that argument settles.

You'll find the ballot on your lineup page too, sitting at the top of the one page everybody in this league visits anyway — same trip, same deadline, no second errand. Twelve of the 24 have to vote or the column runs the machine's numbers alone and says so, which would be a bleak look for a league that argues this much.

Ballots stay sealed until the poll closes, then every one of them publishes. There is a voters page keeping the receipts — who voted, how often, and how well they actually read the league, because every ballot gets scored against how the next week plays out. Being loudly wrong in Week 2 is now a thing that follows you to Week 15. Want a nudge when the ballot opens or a warning before it shuts? Notifications has both, and they're yours to switch on.
imageAlt: The Owners' Poll ballot page on the AFL. A card headed "Rank your top 10 · Week 1" shows "9 of 24 ballots in" and "Closes Thursday, 4:00 PM PDT", with numbered slots filled — Ninjas, Balls Deep, Vitside, Titsburgh, Suh girls, Indians — each with its franchise crest, a team-colored accent bar, and up/down/remove controls.

title: Your Clock Now Follows You Off the Sunday Ticket Board
imageAlt: The Preferences page with Australia and Sydney selected, a preview line reading "Mon 3:00 AM AEST · 10:00 AM PT" and "Sunday Ticket via Kayo Sports", beside an open nav drawer with Preferences pinned under Notifications
summary: The country and clock you set on Preferences used to steer exactly one page. Now the draft's start time, the waiver window, the ballot deadline and the mock-draft lobby all read in your clock with the league's PT beside it — and Preferences has moved into the nav so you can actually find it.
description: We shipped Preferences so you could tell us where you watch from and which clock you live in. Then we used it on precisely one page. Everywhere else the site went on printing Pacific at you and letting you do the arithmetic — which, if you are the owner in Sydney, means every waiver deadline in the league arrived as a subtraction problem.

That is fixed. The draft's start time on the draft hub, the waiver window across the top of Free Agents and inside the claim modal, the ballot deadline on The Pecking Order, the session times in the mock-draft lobby, the "data as of" stamp on the AFL's keeper report — all of them now read in the clock you picked, with the league's PT beside it. A Wednesday 8:00 PM PT waiver deadline reads Thu 1:00 PM AEST · Wed 8:00 PM PT from Sydney, which is the useful version: it tells you it is not even Wednesday where you are.

Your country got the same promotion. The game-day hero on the homepage used to name American networks at everybody — Prime Video, ESPN, CBS/FOX — regardless of whether those channels exist where you are. It now names the channel that actually carries the game where you are: Sky Sports in the UK, Kayo in Australia, DAZN in Canada, FOX México and ESPN México south of the border. Which service sells you the whole slate is a longer answer than a hero has room for, and it stays where it has always lived — on the Sunday Ticket board, one badge per window.

One deliberate piece of restraint: if you have never opened the picker, nothing about your site changed. No clock was guessed for you and none was bolted onto your screens — you stay on the league's PT exactly as before. The second clock shows up the moment you choose one, and not a render sooner. And Preferences now sits in the nav right under Notifications, so finding it no longer requires knowing it exists.

title: Sunday Ticket Now Speaks British and Mexican
imageAlt: The Sunday Ticket board with five country chips — United States, Canada, Australia, United Kingdom, Mexico — with the United Kingdom selected, a Channel 5 line underneath, kickoffs reading 6:00 PM BST, and the Sky Sports mark on every game
summary: The Sunday Ticket board now has a United Kingdom and a Mexico view alongside the US, Canada and Australia — kickoffs in London and Mexico City clocks, and every game badged with the channel that actually carries it there: Sky Sports, Channel 5, FOX México, ESPN México, TUDN and NFL Game Pass, marks and all.
description: One of our owners watches from Great Britain, where 1:00 PM ET is a 6:00 PM kick and CBS does not exist. Until now the Sunday Ticket board told him a game was on FOX at 10:00 AM Pacific, which is true of nobody in his living room.

So the country strip has grown two chips. Pick United Kingdom and every kickoff reads in one London clock — 6:00 PM BST for the early window, 9:25 PM for the late one — and every box wears the Sky Sports mark, because Sky carries the lot over there, RedZone included. The window header swaps YouTube TV for NFL Game Pass on DAZN. Pick Mexico and the slate splits the way it actually splits: FOX México has the Sunday and Thursday package, ESPN México the Sunday and Monday night games, TUDN / ViX the free ones, Game Pass everything else — with two clocks, Mexico City and Tijuana.

There is one thing a network map can never say: which of Sunday's games the free channel picks up is that channel's call, not the American network's. So the board now says it in words, under the country chips — Channel 5's two free Sunday games in the UK, ViX and Canal 5's in Mexico, and 7mate's in Australia, which had been sitting in the config unsaid since the board shipped. Typing UK instead of GB lands you in the right place too; it used to quietly send you back to the American board.

title: Pick The Clock You Actually Live In.
summary: Preferences is a new page: pick the country whose channels you see and the one time zone you live in. Every kickoff on Sunday Ticket prints in your clock, with Pacific — the clock lineup locks and auction windows run on — beside it. Signed in, it follows you to your phone.
description: Sunday Ticket has known which country you watch from since the day it launched — CBS becomes DAZN in Canada, everything is Kayo in Australia. What it did not know was the clock on your wall. Pick the United States and you got Eastern and Pacific, whether you were in Chicago, Denver or Honolulu. Half the league has been doing time-zone arithmetic on a page whose entire job is telling you when to sit down.

The new Preferences page fixes that. Choose your country — it still decides the channel on every box and which service carries Sunday Ticket — and then choose the one time zone you live in. Central. Mountain. Arizona, which refuses to change its clocks and now gets a line of its own. Newfoundland, half an hour off from everybody. Perth, where the early window is a Monday. Whatever you pick, your league's PT rides along beside it, because Pacific is the clock lineup locks and auction windows actually run on. Already on Pacific? Then you get PT once, not twice.

Every kickoff time on the board reads that way now — the window headers, the jump links, the four multiview boxes, the national games underneath. Set it once. It sticks to the browser you set it in, and if you're signed in it's saved to your account too, so the phone you check from the couch reads the same clock as the laptop you set your lineup on. A few of you we already knew about — the Wabbits and the Dream up in Canada, Maverick keeping Sydney hours — and your board comes up right the first time without touching a thing.

The country chips on the Sunday Ticket board still work exactly as they did, and now land right back in your preferences. Nothing about where you actually are gets stored; the schedule is the schedule, we just do the arithmetic for you. Sunday Ticket is the first page to ask. It won't be the last — anything that names a channel or prints a kickoff can read the same two answers.
imageAlt: The Preferences page: the country picker with United States selected, the United States time zone list below it with Eastern chosen, and a preview reading a 1:00 PM ET Sunday kickoff as 1:00 PM ET and 10:00 AM PT

title: Claim Him From Wherever You Found Him
summary: The Bid / Claim button has left the Free Agents table and moved into the player card — so any free agent you turn up anywhere on the site, on any page, can be added right there, next to Watch.
description: Until this week, adding a free agent meant being on one specific page. The button lived in a column on Free Agents and nowhere else, so a name you stumbled across in a matchup, on someone's roster, or halfway down a Schefter Report post was a name you had to go and look up again somewhere else before you could do anything about him.

Now it is wherever he is. Tap a player's name and the card that opens carries two buttons side by side: Watch player, and — if he is genuinely available to you — Claim player in the AFL, Bid player in TheLeague. Same claim form, same drop picker, same waiver window; it just comes to you instead of the other way round.

That last condition is doing real work. The button only appears when the player is actually unrostered in your league, in your conference, and you have a roster to drop from — the AFL holds the same man once in each conference, so "free" there is a per-conference question, not a league-wide one. Anyone already rostered, and anyone you could not file for anyway, simply gets Watch. Nothing about who may claim whom has changed: the same server checks run on submit as always, against MFL rather than against anything the page believed.

On the Free Agents table itself, the pill that used to sit beside the ⋮ is gone and the ⋮ column now says what it does — Claim, or Bid — with the claim, the sign-in for signed-out visitors, and Watch all inside it. One column instead of two, on a table that already scrolls sideways on a phone.
imageAlt: The AFL player card open on free agent Jacoby Brissett, with Watch player and Claim player side by side above his projected points

title: Bid, Claim, Watch. One Tap, No Scrolling.
summary: On Free Agents the Bid or Claim button now sits right beside the player's name, and the ⋮ menu has grown a Bid / Claim option of its own — so on a phone you can file a claim, or start watching a guy, without scrolling the table sideways to find the button.
description: Week 1 waivers found it: on a phone, the one button that does anything on Free Agents — Bid in TheLeague, Claim in the AFL — lived in the last column of a table nine columns wide. Every claim started with a sideways scroll past age, bye week and three kinds of points to reach it. The ⋮ menu that arrived with My Watch List was parked out there with it.

Both now sit right after the player's name, ahead of Age, where a thumb can reach them. And the ⋮ sheet does more than watch: tap it on any free agent and the first option is Bid on this player or Claim this player — the same claim form, the same drop picker, opened from the sheet instead of the button. Signed out? That option opens the sign-in and brings you back to that player with the claim still pending. Watch player sits right underneath, so scouting a guy and striking on him are one tap apart, and every post about him in the Schefter Report lights up the moment you do.

Nothing about the claim itself changed. Whoever may file for a player — and whoever may not — is decided exactly as before; the sheet just reads the button the page already drew for you and does what it does. A rostered player's sheet is still Watch alone.
imageAlt: The AFL free agents page with the ⋮ action sheet open on a free agent, showing Claim this player above Watch player

title: The Handshake Now Knows More Than One Thing
summary: That handshake in the corner used to have exactly one job: tell you somebody offered you a trade. It now opens a Transaction Hub — trade offers and the waiver claims you have filed, plus, in a league that runs a priority order, your live spot in it. A number on the handshake still means somebody is waiting on you. A quiet dot means there is something in there worth a look.
description: First, so nobody goes hunting for the wrong thing: it is this one, <svg class="wn-inline-icon" viewBox="2 26 124 76" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"><use href="/assets/icons/sprite.svg#icon-transactions-2"></use></svg> — the little handshake in the top bar, next to the search glass. Not a bell. It has been sitting up there for months doing one thing. Somebody offers you a trade, it lights up red, you go look. Useful, and also a strange amount of real estate for a single notification.

So it got more rooms. Tap it now and you land on a hub: Trade Offers and Waiver Claims, each with its own count, each one tap deep — plus Waiver Priority in the leagues that actually have one. Trade offers work exactly as they did — accept, reject, dismiss, open it in the Trade Builder to check the cap damage before you say yes.

Waiver Claims shows what you have in, in the order MyFantasyLeague will actually process it — who you are adding, who you are dropping for him, what you bid. It is read-only on purpose. Deleting a claim or swapping the drop still lives on Free Agents, next to the roster and the search you need to do either one, and there is a link straight there at the bottom of the screen. This is the answer to "wait, did I actually put that claim in" at 11pm on a Tuesday, which is a different question from "let me redo my whole board".

Waiver Priority shows up in the AFL, and not in The League, and that is a feature rather than an oversight. The hub asks MyFantasyLeague which waiver system your league runs and believes the answer. The AFL runs rolling priority, so it gets the screen: the live order, read the moment you open it rather than off a nightly sync, your row badged, renumbered within your own conference — because sitting 13th league-wide while being first in the National is not 13th at anything. The League runs blind bidding with ties broken first come first served, so there is no order to stand in. MyFantasyLeague will still hand out a waiver number for it, which is exactly the trap: it is a default nobody set and nothing reads, and putting it on screen would have invented a queue for sixteen owners. If the commissioner ever flips that setting, the screen appears on its own.

One deliberate restraint: the red number on the handshake still counts trade offers and nothing else. A trade is somebody waiting on you. A claim you filed yourself is not, so it gets a small quiet dot instead — the hub has something in it, no one is holding a stopwatch. Turning every claim into a red badge is how the handshake stops meaning anything.
imageAlt: The Transaction Hub modal open over the AFL standings page, headed "Transaction Hub" and "Everything you have in flight". Three rows: Trade Offers, 2 waiting on you, badged 2; Waiver Claims, 2 filed, badged 2; and Waiver Priority, American League, chipped #2.

title: Keep An Eye On Him. Literally.
summary: My Watch List is live, and it is the same list MFL keeps under your name. Watch anyone from a roster, the free-agent pool, or your rankings board, and every Schefter post about him lights up — with a Watching tab to see nothing else, and a push alert if you want one.
description: Every owner has a mental list. The rookie you almost drafted. The receiver whose target share you check every Monday. The running back one injury away from a job. Until now that list lived in your head, or worse, in a note on your phone that you last opened in August.

Now it lives on the site, and it lives on MFL — it IS MFL's My Watch List, so a player you watch here is watched there and back. Tap the ⋮ on any player on the free agents page, any roster in the league (yes, other people's), or your custom rankings board, hit Watch player, and he is on the list. The player card everywhere on the site carries the same switch. One tap adds, one tap removes, nothing to sync and nothing to push.

Then the list starts working for you. The Schefter Report now flags any post about a player you watch — a signing, a cut, a trade, a rumor, a wire story — with a chip naming him, and a new Watching tab shows only those. Your own roster counts automatically, so the tab is your team's news and your shopping list in one scroll. On the free agents page a My Watch List view filters the pool to your list, with a toggle for who is still available and who got scooped.

And if you would rather not scroll at all, the notification center has a new switch: News on your watch list. Off by default, because it is your list and your phone. But flip it, and the moment Schefter posts about one of your guys, so does your lock screen.
imageAlt: The free agents page in the My Watch List view, with the player action sheet open on a watched player showing the Stop watching option

title: The Hardware Went Home With The Owners
summary: AFL owner pages now wear the league's actual trophies — AFL Champion, the AL and NL crowns, every division badge, the NIT, Premier League and D-League — and for the first time that includes the titles won by owners who left before 2016, which the record had been quietly filing under nobody.
description: The AFL has handed out 192 pieces of hardware since 2003, and until this week 59 of them were sitting in a drawer marked defunct. The trophy case on every franchise page is scoped to the current owner, which is correct — the Muck Juggling Micks did not win Delirium Tremens' 2011 title — but it meant that once an owner left, their championship left with them. Way More Funner's 2007 NL East. No Frills' 2008 championship. Brady's Bastards in 2009. Real seasons, real banners, no page.

Now every owner page carries the league's own award badges, in the same art the franchise trophy rooms use, next to the record and the season table. Current owners get the full set at a glance; former owners get theirs back. Jim Shea's page finally says what a dozen seasons of Delirium Tremens earned: one AFL Championship, three NL titles, three division badges. The Record Book is unchanged, and so are the franchise pages — nothing moved, it just finally got delivered.

The trick was one missing number. Before 2016 the AFL was rebuilt as a fresh MFL league every season, so a team's slot number meant nothing from year to year and the award ledger only recorded who to credit today. Every award now also records the slot that actually won it that season, which is enough to place it on whoever held that slot that year — no guessing, no renaming history.
imageAlt: Jim Shea's AFL owner page showing the career record alongside a row of award badge chips: AFL Champion, NL Champion ×3, NL West ×2 and NL Pacific

title: Four Boxes, Two Windows, Every League You're In
summary: Sunday Ticket gives you four boxes per window and no opinion about which games belong in them. The new Sunday Ticket page has one: the games with the most of your starters on the field, ranked, with the real network on each, RedZone in any open box — and it counts your other leagues too.
description: There is a version of Sunday afternoon where you have the multiview up, four boxes lit, and you are watching the one game that has none of your guys in it because you set it up at 9:58 with a coffee in one hand. The Sunday Ticket page is the fix. It looks at every game kicking off in the 1 PM ET window and again in the 4 PM ET window, counts how many of your starters are in each one, and hands you the four to put on. Fewer than four? RedZone takes the open box, which is what you were going to do anyway.

It reads your submitted lineup, so a bench player does not get a box a starter should have — and if you haven't set one yet it says so and works from the roster. Each box lists your players with that league's projection, and the network chip is the real one from the broadcast schedule, not a guess: CBS is CBS, FOX is FOX, and the Thursday, Sunday night and Monday night games sit in their own row underneath, because those are not on the package and pretending otherwise is how you end up flipping to a channel you don't have.

The part that took the longest is the part you'll notice second. If you're in both of our leagues — or in three others somewhere else on MFL — the board counts all of them. Sign in once and every league your account belongs to shows up as a chip across the top; toggle any of them off and the four boxes re-rank. A quarterback you start in two leagues is two reasons to watch that game, and the board says so.

Once the early games kick off the page hands you a link to Live Scoring, which is where Sunday actually happens. Saturday morning and Sunday before 10 is when this one earns its keep. The homepage's “Your Sunday Ticket” panel now points here too — its “Full Preview” button has been a dead link for longer than anyone wants to admit.
imageAlt: The Sunday Ticket page: a 2×2 multiview grid for the early window with four games, each listing the owner's starters, projections and the network, and a RedZone box filling the late window

title: The Room Gets A Vote
summary: Every Tuesday The Pecking Order ranks the league by the numbers. Now you get a say. Rank your top 7 — your own team included, if you think you belong — and the consensus runs in Tuesday's column right next to the algorithm. The week's real story is the room versus the machine.
description: For two years The Pecking Order has ranked this league with math: half all-play record, half rolling three-week scoring, no opinions involved. It has been right often enough to be annoying and wrong often enough to be worth arguing with. The arguing has been happening in the group chat, where it dies.

So now it happens on the record. The ballot opens with the column every Tuesday and closes Thursday at the week's first kickoff — not Wednesday night, deliberately. Setting a lineup is the one thing everybody in this league reliably does, and it mostly happens Wednesday through Sunday, so a Wednesday deadline was asking you to make a second trip. Now it's the same trip: there's a ballot strip on your lineup page, and you can vote from there without going anywhere.

You rank seven of sixteen. First pick is worth 7 points, seventh is worth 1, every ballot counts the same, and you may absolutely rank yourself — that is not a loophole anybody is closing. It is the entire source of the Homer Index, which measures how much higher you rated your own team than the room did, and which is going to make somebody very famous around here. Eight ballots are needed for a consensus to publish; below that the column runs on the numbers alone and everybody knows why.

Ballots stay sealed until the poll closes, then all of them publish. There is a voters page keeping the receipts: who voted, how often, and how well they actually read the league — every ballot is scored against how the season plays out, so being loudly wrong in Week 3 is a thing that follows you to Week 14. The Contrarian Index is there too, for the owner whose ballot agrees with nobody. Sometimes that owner is the only one who saw it coming.

The chat will not be nagging you about this. It gets one automated post a day now, total, and the poll has to share that budget with everything else — so the reminders come to your phone instead, and only if you asked for them, on the notifications page. Ballot opens, ballot closing, where the room put your team. Turn on the ones you want and ignore the rest.
imageAlt: The Owners' Poll ballot page on The League. A commissioner strip reads "Ballot open · Week 1 · 5/16 in"; below it a card headed "Rank your top 7 · Week 1" shows "5 of 16 ballots in" and "Closes Thursday, 10:00 AM PDT", with seven numbered slots filled — Wabbits, Magicians, Dangsters, Vitside, Pain, Pigskins, CPU Jocks — each with its franchise crest, a team-colored accent bar, and up/down/remove controls.

title: Fourteen Ways To Be Told, And You Pick
summary: The group chat now gets one automated post a day. Everything else moved to your phone — trade offers, a broken lineup before kickoff, injuries to your guys, the rumor mill, your final score. Fourteen alert types, four groups, four on by default, and every single one is a switch you own.
description: The league had a volume problem, and it was us. Six bots with something to say and one group chat to say it in is how a chat gets muted, and a muted chat is worse than a quiet one — the deadline reminder that actually mattered went into the same silence as the fourth waiver-claim announcement of the afternoon.

So the chat is now rationed. One automated post a day, on a fixed weekly calendar, and that's the whole budget. Anything a human types is exempt, and so is Roger answering a rules question or reminding you about a deadline — those were never the problem. Everything else moved somewhere you can actually control it.

That somewhere is Notifications, and it is now a proper command center. Fourteen alert types in four groups: things waiting on your team, the Owners' Poll, league news, and game day. Four are on by default — a trade offer, a broken starting lineup while there's still time to fix it, a league deadline, and where the room ranked you. Those four are the ones that cost you something if you miss them. The other ten are off, sitting there, waiting for you to decide you want them.

The new arrivals are worth a look. News on your players watches the injury report and tells you when a status changes on someone you actually roster — including when a guy is CLEARED, which is the version you want on a Saturday when you're deciding whether to start him. Your final score lands when your matchup is genuinely over, per matchup, so a Sunday-only week doesn't make you wait on somebody else's Monday-night kicker. And close-game swings only fires once the early window is done and the lead actually changes hands — because a lead change at 10:30 in the morning, with eleven starters yet to play, is not a result. It's noise, and we're done sending noise.

Turn on everything. Turn on nothing. Turn on the firehose — Every transaction is right there and it is genuinely a firehose, dozens some weeks, and if that's your idea of a good time nobody here is going to stop you. The point is that it's your call now instead of ours.
imageAlt: The Notifications command center on The League, headed "Choose your alerts" and reading "4 of 14 on". The "Your team" group is expanded with Turn all on beside it: Trade offers, Lineup problems before kickoff and League deadlines are switched on and badged ON BY DEFAULT, and News on your players is switched off. The Owners' Poll group begins below.

title: The AFL Can Finally Find Its Own Stuff
summary: There are 42 pages on the AFL site and, until today, exactly one way to reach most of them: remember they exist. The magnifying glass in the header now opens a searchable index of every one — type "bracket", "keeper", "who owns" and it surfaces.
description: The League has had a search page for a year. The AFL has had a nav drawer and a good memory. That was fine when there were a dozen pages; there are now 42, and the honest truth is that some of the best ones — the pecking order, the schedule strength report, the head-to-head rivalries — were effectively invisible unless someone linked you.

So the magnifying glass is now in the AFL header too, on every page, right where it is on the other site. It opens a card for every page the AFL has, each with its own description and tags. Type a word and it filters as you go — by title, by description, by tag, by category — and it sorts what is left by how much people actually use it. You do not have to know what a page is called. "Money", "bracket", "trade", "who won in 2014" all land somewhere sensible.

The five chips across the top — Popular, My Team, Reports, Tools, Info — filter without typing anything, which is the better move when you are browsing rather than hunting. And the “All pages” link on the AFL homepage now goes here instead of bouncing you back to the homepage you were already on.

One thing it will never do is show you TheLeague's pages. The page index is a single shared list across both sites, so the AFL's copy is scoped to AFL routes only — no contracts, no salary cap, no dead money, none of the things this league does not have. What you see is what you can click.
imageAlt: The AFL Search page. A heading reads Search with “42 pages” beside it and the subtitle “Find any page on the site by name, category, or keyword.” Below it a search box reads “Search pages... (e.g. money, bracket, trade)”, then a row of category chips — Popular, My Team, Reports, Tools, Info. Under those, a three-column grid of cards, each with an icon, a page title, a one-line description and a row of tags: AFL Throwback Week Settings, AFL Notification Settings, AFL Live Scoring, Record Book, Search, Rosters, Free Agents, Standings, Set Lineup, Keepers, Keeper Report Card, Playoffs, Schefter Report, Trade Builder and Draft Order.

title: The AFL Mock Draft Knows Who You Kept
summary: Nine rounds against the clock, drafting from the players your conference actually left unkept — not a generic board, not last year's names. It opens when the keeper cuts land in July and closes when the real draft starts, because those are the only weeks it tells you anything true.
description: The League has had a mock draft for a while. Running the same thing for the AFL would have been a morning's work and completely useless, because the AFL doesn't draft rookies off a fixed board — it drafts whoever twelve owners decided not to keep. A mock that doesn't know that is just a list of famous people.

So this one starts from your keepers and works backwards. Every draftable player, minus the seven each of your conference's twelve teams held onto. What's left is the board — and this year that's a little over eleven hundred names in the American League, which is a real number rather than a round one.

The part that took the longest is the part nobody will notice. MyFantasyLeague lets a player sit on one roster per conference, and the AFL leans on that hard: of the eighty-four men the AL kept this July, sixty are also kept in the National League. The same guy went first overall in both drafts. So the pool subtracts your conference's rosters and only yours — do it league-wide and you quietly delete twenty-four players the AL is perfectly free to draft, and the board still looks fine, which is the worst kind of wrong.

It also drafts in the right shape. Nine rounds, and the same order every round — no snake, because the AFL doesn't snake — pulled straight from MFL's own slots so traded picks land where they really land. The bots pick off redraft ADP, or dynasty, or your own draft list, or pure chaos if you want to see what happens when the room loses its mind. You pick your conference at the top, the same way the draft room does.

And it tells you when it's not worth running. Before the cuts, the board is still holding a hundred players who are about to be released, so it stays shut and names the teams it's waiting on. Once the real draft starts, it shuts again and points you at the big board. The window is roughly mid-July to draft weekend — which, if you were wondering why it's closed today, is the honest answer. It's sitting with the rest of the tools on the draft hub, next to the order, one click away.
imageAlt: The AFL Mock Draft room, opened on the American League. Breadcrumbs read Home / Draft / Mock Draft / Session, above a row of draft tabs — Draft, Order, Results, Broadcast, Room, Mock, Rankings, My List — with Mock highlighted in red. A note beneath reads that the board is drafting from the American League's available pool and that players kept in the NL are still draftable here. A dark banner says “Waiting for draft to begin…” with Go Back, Pause and Reset Draft buttons. Under it the draft board offers nine round tabs, Rd 1 through Rd 9, with Rd 1 selected, and tabs for Players, Queue and Chat. The Players pane is headed AVAILABLE with a count of 1109, a search box, position filters, and a list of available players led by C.J. Stroud, Sam Darnold and Malik Willis.

title: Know Where You Are In Line
summary: The AFL runs rolling waiver priority, which means every claim you file is really a bet on how many teams pick before you do. That number was on MyFantasyLeague and nowhere else. Now it's a button on Free Agents — your conference's order, live, with your team outlined and everyone ahead of you named.
description: Priority waivers are a queue, and a queue you can't see is just a rumour. You'd put in for a running back on Free Agents, feel reasonably good about it, and find out Monday night that four teams ahead of you felt reasonably good about him too. The number that decided all of it — where you sit in the order — lived on MyFantasyLeague, behind a login, on a page nobody opens on purpose.

So there's a Waiver priority button at the top of Free Agents now. It reads the order straight out of MyFantasyLeague when you open it, not from something we cached last Tuesday, because priority is rolling — win a claim and you drop to the back, which is rather the point of the system. Your team is outlined in the list. Everyone ahead of you is named.

It shows your conference and only your conference, and that's deliberate rather than lazy. The American and National leagues each roster their own copy of every player, so an American owner has never once competed with a National owner for a claim. MyFantasyLeague stores the two orders as one long list of 24, which means the National team sitting at number 13 is actually first in line — show anyone that raw number and you've told them a lie about their own odds.

Count the names above yours and you have your answer: that many players can be gone before your turn comes round, so line up at least one more target than that. Then file them from the same page — the Claim button is right there in every row, and the claims you've already filed sit just above the table.
imageAlt: The Waiver priority modal over the AFL Free Agents page, listing the twelve American League teams in claim order with Smokane FC outlined and badged YOU at number 10

title: The Last Trip To MFL, Cancelled
summary: Land on Free Agents without signing in and the acquire button used to fling you at MyFantasyLeague in a new tab, which is a strange thing for a site built to replace MyFantasyLeague to do. Now it opens a sign-in right there, and drops you back on the same page — on the same player — ready to bid.
description: There was one door left open to the old building. Every row on Free Agents carries a button to go get the player, and if you weren't signed in, that button was a deep link to MyFantasyLeague's add/drop page. New tab, second login, different UI, and your afternoon's research left behind in a tab you'd stopped looking at. Signed-in owners have been bidding in place since the start of the month; everyone else was still being shown the exit.

Now the button opens our own sign-in, right on top of the page you're already reading. Same MyFantasyLeague credentials — they go straight to MFL and we never keep your password — but you stay here. When it clears, the page comes back exactly where you left it, filters and all, and the bid form opens on the player you clicked in the first place. No hunting back through 600 free agents for the tight end you'd talked yourself into.

One thing still points at MyFantasyLeague on purpose: bidding during the offseason auction. That's MFL's own live auction, and signing in here wouldn't get you into it — so during auction season the link stays a link, and says so.
imageAlt: The sign-in modal open over TheLeague's Free Agents page in dark mode, asking for MFL username and password with the note that credentials are validated directly with MyFantasyLeague

title: Your Tip Now Tells You How It Ended
summary: Send a tip and it either turns into a rumor or it doesn't — and until now, "doesn't" looked exactly like a broken tip line. Your record card on the tip page now carries a receipt for your last tip: it ran, it got spiked, or it aged out.
description: Here is what filing a tip used to feel like. You'd write something up on the tip page, hit send, get a cheerful "Schefter's got it" — and then nothing. Maybe a rumor showed up on the feed a few hours later. Maybe it never did. There was no way to tell the difference between a tip Schefter passed on and a tip line that had quietly stopped working, which is a rough way to treat the people doing the reporting.

So your record card now shows a receipt for your most recent tip, and it says one of three things. It made the wire — with a link straight to the rumor it became. It got spiked — Schefter ran it, couldn't find an angle he was willing to print, and let it go. Or it aged out — nothing wrong with the tip, the wire was just quiet and it never got picked up before it expired.

The spiked note is the useful one, because it comes with the actual editorial standard attached: tips carrying a name, a number, or a deadline clear the bar far more often than tips carrying a vibe. "Somebody's shopping a receiver" is a shrug. "They want a second for the receiver before Sunday" is a story.

Nothing about this touches your anonymity. The receipt is filed against the same one-way hash your codename hangs on, it only ever loads for you, and it clears itself out after two weeks. Schefter still doesn't know who you are, and neither do we.
imageAlt: The Tip Schefter page with the Your Record card in the right rail showing a spiked receipt: 'Your last tip didn't make the wire — Schefter couldn't find an angle he could print.'

title: The AFL Gets A Draft Room, Twice
summary: A live board for your conference's draft — the picks as they land, who's on the clock, the pool, your queue and the room chat. It opens on YOUR conference, because the AL and the NL are two different drafts that happen to share a season, and the last thing an NL owner needs on draft weekend is a screen full of the AL's picks.
description: The League has had a draft room for two years. The AFL has had a spreadsheet's worth of browser tabs. That ends now — with one wrinkle that took longer to get right than the room itself.

The AFL doesn't hold a draft. It holds two. The American League gets in a room, sets a clock and picks in front of each other. The National League runs an email draft that unspools over days while people are at work. Same season, same rules, completely different events — and MyFantasyLeague only records one setting for the whole league, so software that trusts the feed gets one of the two wrong every time.

So the room asks which draft you mean, and then commits to it. Land on it as an NL owner and you get the NL board, the NL's twelve teams, a clock that counts in hours because that's how your draft actually moves, and a button that opens MFL's email-draft page. Land on it as an AL owner and you get a clock in minutes and the live draft applet. Switch to the other conference whenever you like — it'll say plainly that you're watching someone else's draft and won't pretend you're on the clock.

Everything else the room already did comes along: the board fills as picks land, the pool sorts by redraft ADP with search and position filters, you can stack a queue, and there's chat. It sits with the rest of the draft tools — the draft hub, the order, the big board and every draft we've ever held — one click from each other along the top.
imageAlt: The AFL Draft Room showing the National League's draft. Across the top, tabs for Draft, Order, Results, Broadcast, Room, Rankings and My List, with Room selected. Below them a Conference row offers two chips — “American League / live draft” and “National League / email draft” — with the National League one highlighted. Two notices follow: “You're watching the National League's draft. You don't pick in this one — switch above for your own conference.” and an explanation that the NL drafts by email over several days so the clock counts in hours. A blue banner reads “ON THE CLOCK · 6.07 — Swiftie 4 Life” with “9h 22m” at the right. Under it the round-6 board shows picks 6.01 through 6.06 already made — Malik Washington, Emmett Johnson, Kenyon Sadiq, Chigoziem Okonkwo, Matthew Golden and Brock Purdy — with 6.07 marked “On the clock”. The player pool beneath lists 1,235 available players led by Jahmyr Gibbs, Bijan Robinson and Ja'Marr Chase.

title: Your Waiver Claims, On Your Own Site
summary: File a claim and it used to vanish into MyFantasyLeague until Monday night told you how it went. Now the claims you have pending sit at the top of Free Agents in the order they'll be awarded, and you can change who you're dropping or scrap one entirely without leaving.
description: Filing was only ever half of it. You'd pick a player on Free Agents, hit submit, and then the claim disappeared into MyFantasyLeague — no way to see what you had pending, no way to change the guy you'd promised to drop, no way to back out of a claim you'd thought better of at 11pm. The only honest answer was to open MFL in another tab and do it there, which rather defeats the point of building any of this.

So the claims you've filed now sit right above the player list, numbered in the order MyFantasyLeague will actually award them. Each one tells you who you're adding, who you're dropping, and which round it's in. Change drop swaps the casualty without touching the claim. Delete takes the whole thing back. Both go straight to MFL and are read back out again before we'll tell you they worked — if we can't confirm it, we say so rather than showing you a checkmark and hoping.

One thing it deliberately won't do: reorder. MyFantasyLeague has no reorder control — we went looking, and the only way to shuffle a round is to delete every claim and re-file them in a new sequence, which leaves a gap where you own nothing at all. That's a lousy trade during a live waiver window, so the priority you see is the order you filed in. Get the order right on the way in, and fix the drops from here. If you'd rather see it all on MFL, the link at the corner of the panel goes straight there.
imageAlt: The Your Waiver Claims panel above the Free Agents table, listing three pending claims numbered by priority with Change drop and Delete buttons on each

title: The Hero Wears Your Colors
summary: Sign in and the big card at the top of the homepage stops being league furniture and starts being yours — your franchise's gradient behind it, your crest sitting dead center, the headline and the player still riding over the top. It's the draft broadcast's reveal treatment, brought home.
description: For two years the top of the homepage has opened the same way for all forty of us. A deep navy card in the AFL, a deep blue one in The League, a red corner glow, a headline, a player cut out and floating on the right. Handsome. Also completely anonymous — the single biggest thing on the page you look at most, and it had nothing to say about who was looking at it.

Sign in now and that card is your franchise's. The background is your team's own gradient — the exact string the draft broadcast paints on the TV when your pick lands, not a second, slightly-different version of it — and your crest sits in the middle of the card at watermark strength, the copy crossing its left edge and the player crossing its right. Smokane opens green under the shield. The Pigskins open red under the pig. Midwestside opens damn near black with a gold ring floating in it, which is exactly right.

Everything on the card moved with it. The accent word, the countdown number, the pill and the border are all your team now, and the button went neutral white with your color as the type — no league gold, no league red, nothing borrowed. The border is the part that took the most fiddling: it runs a lighter cut of your color in dark mode and a deeper one in light, so the card lifts off the page either way instead of dissolving into it on one of them.

None of that is hand-picked, and it can't be — there are forty franchises and two themes, so somebody's headline was always going to end up unreadable if these were eyeballed. Every color is measured before it ships: the accent has to clear the contrast floor against the exact gradient it lands on, AND stay far enough from white that it still reads as an accent instead of melting into the headline around it. The pill's label is small type, so it's held to the stricter bar. A few teams needed a nudge lighter or deeper to get there and got one. Four franchises — Bring The Pain, Wabs, and the AFL's two — have no color in their palette at all, just black and white, so they get a bright silver, which is the honest answer rather than a hue nobody chose.

Two deliberate holdouts. Signed out, you get the league chrome exactly as it was — there is no team to wear, and a generic gradient pretending to be one is worse than honest navy. Picking a team on the AFL with the team switcher doesn't do it either: that sets which team the page is ABOUT, and a card in your colors is saying the site is yours, which should take an actual login. And the heroes that are ABOUT somebody else keep their own colors: the playoff bracket, the champion card, the live scoreboard and the weekly matchup already wear whoever is in them, and painting your red over a card announcing another owner's title would be a strange way to congratulate him.
imageAlt: The AFL homepage hero for a signed-in Smokane FC owner. The whole card is in Smokane's green: a green gradient background with Smokane's gas-mask shield crest watermarked large across the middle, a lighter green border, a green star chip and a green AFL pill. The headline reads “TWO CONFERENCES. ONE.” with ONE in the same mint green rather than the AFL's gold, above a two-line summary and a neutral-white VIEW STANDINGS button whose label is a deep green. Joe Burrow's cutout headshot floats on the right above a frosted caption reading Joe Burrow, HEADLINER · QB · CIN.

title: The AFL Gets a Throwback Week
summary: On NFL Week 8, all 24 AFL franchises drop their current look and wear a legacy one — old name, old crest, old banner, old colors — across live scoring, matchups and Set Lineup. A hundred and seventeen eras going back to 2003 are on the table, and you pick which one is yours.
description: The AFL has been keeping receipts since 2003. Every name this league has ever worn is sitting in the config — 117 of them, across 24 franchises — and until now they only ever surfaced on franchise pages as history. On NFL Week 8 they come out of the drawer. Live scoring, the matchup cards and Set Lineup all swap to whatever era you picked, and everybody else's too.

Swiftie 4 Life has thirteen identities to choose between, which is its own kind of confession. Get off my Ditka has nine. Nobody has to settle — pick your era and it sticks until you change it, and there's a Preview link on every card so you can see the scoreboard wearing it before you commit. Skip the whole thing and you still play: every team already has a default, and it's the identity you wore the LONGEST. The Show spent seventeen seasons as No Frills, so that's what The Show wears.

One rule about the defaults, because it matters. A last-place rebrand is never picked for you. Finishing last in this league gets you renamed, and the site is not going to turn around and make that your throwback too — Cock Gobbler, Jesus Killers, Vit's Brother and the rest are all still there in the picker if you want to own it, but you have to reach for them yourself.

Two teams nearly missed the party. Drunk Indians and Fullybaked have never once changed their names in twenty-two years, so their history was empty and they had nothing to throw back to. Turned out MFL never deleted anything: the original art was still sitting on the same servers it was uploaded to in 2003, down to a Half Baked movie poster tiled four across at exactly the width of a league banner, because that is how you made a banner in 2003. Both are in, wearing the real thing.

A word of warning about the names. This league was not tasteful in 2004 and nobody has asked it to be now, so the Week 8 scoreboard is going to say some things. Every era is eligible. That was the point.
imageAlt: The AFL live scoring board during Throwback Week. Every franchise wears a legacy identity instead of its current one: No Frills against Way More Funner in the featured matchup, then Gamecocks over TD Pants, Smokane over Drunk Indians, Fullybaked over The Dude, More Cowbell against Pubes, MWC over The Nukes, and Your Team Sucks over Zephyr. Each team shows its era crest and every matchup card is edged in that era's own colors.
